l: work of the body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The work of the body includes the stomach preparing food, the blood carrying food and removing worn-out matter, the lungs using fresh air to purify the blood, and the skin carrying away waste matter. This work continues day and night without conscious thought because nerves send messages to the muscles.

l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The unit explains the five senses, with special attention to sight and hearing. It describes how the eyes, pupils, nerves of sight, ears, and nerve of hearing work, and teaches care of the eyes and ears. Stories about boys who looked at the sun, a boy who made himself cross-eyed, and the boy's father illustrate the dangers of injuring these organs. It also explains that alcohol can weaken the work of all the senses.

l: the five senses, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The five senses are sight, touch, taste, smell, and hearing. They are ways of learning about things around a person.

l: sight, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Sight is one of the five senses and depends on the eyes and the nerve of sight. Its delicate nerves can be harmed by too much or too little light.

l: hearing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Hearing is one of the five senses and depends on the ears and the nerve of hearing. It can be harmed by putting hard or sharp objects into the ears.

l: the eyes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The eyes take pictures of things and send accounts of what is seen to the brain. They need protection from very bright light, insufficient light, and careless actions.

l: the pupil, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The pupil is a round, black opening in the middle of the eye, with a muscle around it. The muscle makes it smaller in bright light and larger in darkness.

l: the nerve of sight, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The nerve of sight is in a little, round room behind the pupil and carries accounts of what is seen to the brain. It is delicate and can be seriously harmed by bright light or trying to see in the dark.

l: the light, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The light should be sufficient for reading and studying but should not be faced directly when it is very bright. While writing, it should come from the left side so that the hand's shadow does not fall on the work.

l: the ears, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The visible ears are pieces of gristle curved to catch sounds and pass them to the true ears deeper in the head. They should be washed with a soft towel and should not have hard or sharp objects put into them.

l: the nerve of hearing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The nerve of hearing is deeper in the head and sends an account of each sound to the brain. It is in less danger than the nerve of sight, but it can be injured when a pin breaks the ear's drum.

l: the boys who looked at the sun, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The boys foolishly tried to see which could look straight at the sun the longest. Their eyes and brains were greatly harmed, and the boy who looked longest died as a result.

l: the boy who made himself cross-eyed, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The boy tried to imitate a schoolmate who was cross-eyed by turning his own eyes. He could not turn them back properly, and doctors were never able to set them quite right despite painful treatment.

l: the boy's father, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The boy's father laid his ear against a door crack to feel the wind blow into it when he was young. He afterward suffered severe earache and often had earache throughout his life.

l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Alcohol can confuse the nerves and weaken the work of touching, tasting, seeing, smelling, and hearing. A person who habitually uses alcoholic drinks may have trembling hands, thick speech, difficulty walking straight, or may think he sees things that are not present.

l: care of the eyes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Care of the eyes requires avoiding direct bright light, having enough light for reading, and positioning light on the left while writing. The eyes should not be strained by looking at the sun, reading in twilight, or imitating crossed eyes.

l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The unit explains that body heat is produced by work inside the body, carried by the blood, and lost through the skin and breath. Exercise increases blood flow and warmth, while clothing helps retain existing heat rather than producing it. Alcohol creates a temporary feeling of warmth by bringing hot blood to the skin, but it increases heat loss and dulls awareness of cold. Accounts of Arctic explorers and the Greely party show that alcohol and tobacco did not help people endure severe cold, hunger, and freezing.

l: heat and cold, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Heat is produced by work inside the body and is carried throughout it by the blood. Cold causes heat to be lost, especially when cool air carries it away from the skin.

l: body heat, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Body heat comes from work that is constantly taking place inside the body. It is carried by the blood and continually passes off through the skin and in the breath.

l: clothing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Clothing keeps existing body heat from escaping and helps prevent cold air from reaching the skin. Woolen under-garments, thick boots, and stockings are recommended for cold weather.

l: children, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: A child is warm inside even when the fingers are cold. Children generally feel warmer than old people because their hearts beat faster, usually eighty to ninety times a minute.

l: blood, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The blood is warmed by work inside the body and carries heat to every part of it. Faster blood flow brings more heat and makes a person feel warmer.

l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The body produces heat through its internal work but loses heat through the skin and breath. When the skin is chilled, perspiration tubes may close and prevent waste matter from leaving properly.

l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Alcohol brings hot blood to the tiny tubes near the skin, creating a temporary feeling of warmth. It actually increases heat loss, dulls the nerves, and can make a person freeze more quickly.

l: Arctic explorers, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Arctic explorers report that alcohol does not keep them warm. They travel through icy regions, sometimes use dog sledges and Esquimau huts, and may drink oil and eat walrus meat.

l: Greely party, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The Greely party consisted of twenty-six men who were rescued from the Arctic seas after months of starving and freezing. Nineteen died, seven were found alive, and one of those seven died soon afterward.

l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Tobacco did not help the men of the Greely party during their hardship. It probably weakened their stomachs and made it harder for them to use poor food effectively.

l: Arctic expedition ordeal, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The Greely party's ordeal involved months of hunger and extreme cold in the Arctic seas. Most of the men died, while those who survived generally had not used tobacco or had used it only seldom.

l: cold exposure and freezing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Cold exposure causes the body to lose heat and can lead to freezing and death. Alcohol may make freezing happen more quickly because it increases heat loss and prevents a person from recognizing the danger.

l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The unit explains that spending money on alcohol or liquor is wasteful because it brings harm rather than useful benefits. It describes how beer, wine, and whiskey can quickly consume a dollar, and says that avoiding liquor could reduce sickness, poverty, crime, and the need for policemen and prisons. It also explains that buying tobacco burns up money while harming the smoker. The unit states that six hundred million dollars are spent on tobacco in the country each year.

l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Alcohol costs a great deal of money. Money spent on alcohol is described as wasted, or worse than wasted, because it does no good and only causes harm.

l: money, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Money can be saved or spent in good and pleasant ways, but spending it on liquor or tobacco wastes it. A dollar spent on two mugs of beer a day is wasted in ten days.

l: wasting money, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Wasted money is money spent on something that does no good but only causes harm. Money spent on liquor or tobacco is presented as wasted or worse than wasted.

l: cost of alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The cost of alcohol can quickly use up a dollar: two mugs of beer a day consume a dollar in ten days, while wine or whiskey use it sooner because they cost more.

l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Tobacco is compared to a dollar bill that is burned up, because buying and smoking it quickly wastes money. Smoking tobacco also hurts the person who uses it.

l: cost of tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: The yearly cost of tobacco in the country is six hundred million dollars. This money is described as burned up, wasted, and worse than wasted.

l: liquor, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Liquor includes beer, wine, and whiskey in the unit's examples of wasteful spending. If no liquor were drunk, men, women, and children would be better and happier, and fewer policemen, jails, and prisons would be needed.

l: six hundred million dollars, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
s: Six hundred million dollars are spent in this country every year for tobacco. The unit describes this amount as money burned up, wasted, and worse than wasted.

l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Child’s Health Primer for Primary Classes, Pathfinder Physiology No. 1, is a primary-school textbook by Jane Andrews on anatomy, physiology, and hygiene. Endorsed by the Scientific Department of the Women’s Christian Temperance Union of the United States, it especially emphasizes the claimed harmful effects of alcoholic drinks, stimulants, narcotics, and tobacco. It uses short lessons, examples, stories, and review questions, with pronunciation guidance in its front matter. The book begins with bones, joints, the spine, ribs, posture, footwear, and warnings about tobacco during growth. It then explains muscles and tendons, exercise and idleness, and the brain, spinal cord, and nerves that direct movement and sensation. These early chapters argue that sleep and rest protect the nervous system while alcohol and tobacco injure it. A central sequence explains alcohol’s production and nature: fruit juice ferments into wine or cider; barley is made into beer; and distillation produces stronger liquors such as brandy, rum, whiskey, and gin. Alcohol is repeatedly presented as a poison that can create desire, drunkenness, weakness, and failure. Tobacco is traced from the farmer’s crop to cigars and snuff, with nicotine described as a strong poison. Opium and soothing-syrup are likewise condemned as narcotics that harm nerves and babies. The later chapters survey organs and bodily processes: teeth, stomach, gastric juice, food, water, salt, lime, digestion, blood, heart, lungs, skin, and the senses. They promote simple food, clean water, exercise, fresh and ventilated air, cleanliness, and care of the eyes and ears. Alcohol and tobacco are linked throughout to injury of digestion, blood, heart, lungs, senses, muscles, nerves, and clear thinking. A discussion of body heat argues that alcohol only gives temporary warmth while increasing heat loss, citing Arctic explorers and the Greely party. The book closes by treating alcohol and tobacco as economic as well as bodily harms. It says money spent on beer, wine, whiskey, and tobacco is wasted and associates liquor with sickness, poverty, crime, policemen, and prisons.

l: Child's Health Primer For Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes is a book and textbook by Jane Andrews for primary classes, suited to pupils of the ordinary third reader grade. It is a simple, practical introduction to anatomy, physiology, and hygiene, concentrating on facts needed to explain health truths and the effects of alcoholic drinks, stimulants, narcotics, tobacco, and opium upon the human system. Beginning with front matter that states its purpose and explains pronunciation codes, it continues with many apt illustrations and review questions. It is endorsed by the Scientific Department of the Women's Christian Temperance Union of the United States.

l: Pathfinder Physiology No. 1, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_a Child's Health Primer Pathfinder Physiology No. 1 identifies Child's Health Primer as the first book in the Pathfinder series of textbooks on anatomy, physiology, and hygiene.

l: Scientific Department of the Women's Christian Temperance Union of the United States, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A department of the Women's Christian Temperance Union of the United States, it endorses Child's Health Primer and the Pathfinder series.

l: alcoholic drinks, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Alcoholic drinks, substances specially referenced for effects on the human system, can become increasingly desirable with use; habitual takers may value them above everything else despite knowing the drinks are ruining them.

l: stimulants, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: affect human system [as described in the primer] Stimulants are among the substances whose effects upon the human system receive special reference in Child's Health Primer.

l: narcotics, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Narcotics are substances affecting the human system by putting nerves to sleep; the primer gives them special reference and identifies alcohol, tobacco, and opium as narcotics.

l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The human body is a possession of every person: a living body with a brain, about two hundred bones, and joints better than those of dolls. Built during childhood, it grows and is repaired as parts wear out. It is a busy workshop whose organs work day and night, including during sleep. Food, carried through the blood, supplies its bones, muscles, nerves, brain, skin, hair, nails, and eyes, supporting growth and mending broken or worn parts. Made largely of water, it needs pure water from drinks and food, as well as salt and fat. Its health depends on pure blood, fresh air, exercise, and good, simple food. The lungs help purify blood; if they cannot take in enough air, the whole body suffers and life may be shortened. Skin covers it and, with the stomach, blood, heart, and lungs, helps prepare food, carry materials, use air, and remove waste. Internal work produces heat, while skin and breath continually lose it.

l: wasting money, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_a illustration Wasted money is money spent on something that does no good but only causes harm. Money spent on liquor or tobacco is presented as wasted or worse than wasted.

l: Primary Schools, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: teach physiology and hygiene [under the education requirement] Primary Schools are identified as the schools for whose children this work was prepared. The book is intended to help teach pupils in these schools about health and the effects of alcoholics and other narcotics.

l: physiology and hygiene, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: concerns human body Physiology and hygiene are taught together in connection with facts about the human body and the preservation of health. The unit presents basic information about bones, joints, muscles, nerves, organs, food, strength, and the effects of harmful substances.

l: health, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_preserved_by correct physical habits Health is connected with the proper care of the body and with avoiding substances that weaken it. The unit advises upright posture, properly fitting shoes, and avoiding tobacco.

l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Alcohol is presented as a popular thin liquid poison, not food that makes a person strong. It is made from grain and fruit when sugar in fruit-juice changes, with yeast helping change sugar into gas and alcohol. It remains mixed with water, mixes readily with it, and becomes vapor with less heat than water requires. In distillation it is collected before water; repeated distillation makes it purer and stronger by increasing the proportion of alcohol. The records emphasize its harm to body, mind, life, and character. Small amounts harm anyone who drinks it, while large amounts can kill. It injures the brain and nerves, may prevent messages from being sent properly, cause headache and carelessness, and makes the person who takes it want more. It changes muscles partly into fat and takes away their strength. It harms the stomach by injuring gastric juice, causing burning in the throat and, with repeated use, sores that may sometimes be fatal. Alcohol may seem to warm a person because it rushes hot blood into tiny tubes near the skin, but this increases heat loss, deadens nerves’ warning of cold, and lessens power to resist cold. Beer, wine, cider, brandy, and other drinks contain it. From its making and strengthening through distillation to its effects on drinkers, it is portrayed as harmful and costly: money spent on it is wasted or worse than wasted because it does no good and causes harm.

l: other narcotics, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: affect human body [harmfully] Other narcotics are included among the substances whose effects on the human system pupils are to study. Opium is specifically listed as one of the subjects treated in the book.

l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Tobacco is a plant with tall growth and broad green leaves, but it is described as a poison and narcotic because it contains nicotine, a strong poison. Its leaves may be pressed into cakes, rolled into cigars, or ground into snuff; working with it can make people pale and sickly. In any form it is called a great enemy to youth: while growing, it weakens the body, stunts growth, harms the mind, and prevents bones from growing as well as they otherwise would. Boys who smoke or chew may remember lessons less well and may have worse manners. Tobacco deadens nerves, so users may not feel cold or tired without being helped. It dries the mouth, increases saliva, discolors teeth, causes mouth sores and often throat disease, poisons blood, and makes air unpleasant and unfit to breathe. During the Greely party's ordeal it was no help and probably weakened stomachs. It also wastes money: buying and smoking it is likened to burning a dollar, with six hundred million dollars spent yearly in this country.

l: opium, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Opium is a popular narcotic poison made from poppy juice. It affects the human body, life, and character, poisoning the body alongside alcohol and tobacco. It is used in medicines and may be put into soothing-syrups; a text addresses it in a separate chapter.

l: children, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Children have about two hundred bones, with more gristle than older people, so their bones bend easily. As they grow, they need food each day for larger bones, muscles, and skin, while their stomachs should rest rather than eat constantly. They are told to sit and stand erect, avoid twisting limbs, and protect growing bodies from tobacco. They are generally warm inside and warmer than old people because their hearts beat eighty to ninety times a minute; cold fingers may be warmed by the mouth. They are better and happier without liquor.

l: boy, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A boy is advised not to use tobacco while growing. Smoking first makes boys sick, though some continue because they think it is manly and become used to it. Tobacco weakens body and mind and prevents him from becoming as large and fine-looking as he otherwise could.

l: joints, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Joints connect bones, allowing the body to bend and move. They include hinge-joints in elbows, knees, fingers, and toes, and ball-and-socket hip-joints. Soft smooth fluid keeps them moist. Two or more muscles, fastened by tendons, move joints as one shortens and another stretches.

l: bones, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Bones form the human body's jointed framework, including the spine, twenty-four ribs, shoulder-blades, collar-bones, and long and short bones. They contain lime and gristle; children’s have more gristle, old people’s more lime and break more easily.

l: spine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The spine is made of twenty-four small bones separated by elastic gristle cushions that absorb jolts; leaning over work can press the cushions out of shape and make a person round-shouldered or hump-backed.

l: lime, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Lime is a mineral component needed by bones; grass and grains take it from earth, and people obtain it through milk, bread, oat-meal porridge, and other foods.

l: lungs, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The lungs are useful organs in the chest, on each side of and beside the heart. Containing air-cells, they work steadily day and night: the cells expand to take in air and contract to send it out. They need fresh air and room to expand and work; bending over cramps them. Using fresh air, they purify dark, impure blood, making it bright, pure, and red, and breathe out impurities as waste matter.

l: tobacco use by youth, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Tobacco use by youth is a great danger because developing bodies and minds are harmed. From ages seven to fourteen, smoking or chewing can stunt growth and prevent full bodily and mental development, leaving less fine body and mind at twenty-one.

l: cigarettes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: are very poisonous [despite being small] Cigarettes are small but are described as very poisonous. The text warns that smoking them can harm growing boys and girls.

l: chewing tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Chewing tobacco is described as a worse, more filthy habit than smoking, causing frequent spitting that disgusts others and harms the chewer's health.

l: muscles, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Muscles are lean meat and strong parts of the body. Fastened to bones by tendons, they move joints by contracting, shortening when a joint bends, and returning to their first shape when it straightens; each joint has two or more muscles. Brain messages and nerves keep muscles working, including quiet, steady breathing muscles. Muscle also makes up the heart and enables it to pump blood. Muscles grow through daily use, exercise, brisk play, work, and food carried by blood, while idleness weakens them. Alcohol may change part of muscles to fat, take away strength, harm muscles, and leave a fatty heart less able to work. Swallows have large, strong breast muscles.

l: people, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: People once thought alcohol and beer gave strength, but the chapter explains that grain’s food has mostly become alcohol. Spending money on liquor is linked with more sickness, poverty, badness, and wretchedness.

l: exercise, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Exercise and active work, including running, coasting, ball games, and brisk play, strengthen growing muscles; idle habits weaken them. In fresh air, exercise also helps purify the blood, makes the heart work well as it beats faster with rests between beats, and warms the body better than a fire.

l: beer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Beer is a drink containing a little alcohol. It is made from barley after starch changes to sugar and yeast helps change the sugar into gas and alcohol; hops may add bitterness. It is not good food and does not provide real strength, though it may cause fleshiness. Drinking much of it can consume much alcohol and make drunkards.

l: fat, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Fat is a food that provides heat and forms body cushions and wrappings for warmth and comfort; it does not increase muscle strength or work joints. Good fat comes from suitable foods, while alcohol makes it badly and wrongly placed.

l: brain, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The brain is the body's central telegraph office: it thinks, receives messages from nerves, sends orders to muscles and the rest of the body, and controls breathing and other automatic work. Protected by a strong box of bone, its thinking part needs quiet sleep and good care. It needs much pure, good blood and may remain useful for seventy or eighty years if well cared for; alcohol in the blood harms control.

l: nerves, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Nerves are little white cords or threads connecting the brain with the rest of the body, many branching from the spinal cord. They carry messages to muscles and provide feeling, including pain and pleasure. They tire from one activity, rest through changed work, and alcohol and tobacco injure or deaden them.

l: spinal cord, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_located_in bony case [made by the spine] The spinal cord is a large cord that lies safely in a bony case made by the spine. Many nerves branch off from it.

l: heart, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The heart is a useful organ in the chest, near the lungs, made of very thick, strong muscle. It receives blood purified by the lungs and pumps it through arteries, tubes, and the body, where the blood carries food and removes worn-out matter before returning through veins. It rests briefly between beats and, in children, pumps eighty to ninety times a minute and works faster than in old people. Exercise helps it work well; alcohol can make it beat too fast, tire it, and make it fatty. It is similar to, but smaller than, a beef's heart.

l: liquor, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Liquor is a beverage that contains alcohol and can be made from corn, rye, or barley; it includes beer, wine, and whiskey. Distilled liquor is nearly one-half alcohol, and strong liquor can injure more quickly than weaker liquor. When drunk frequently, liquor can slowly poison the body and reduce recovery from sickness. It is presented as wasteful spending linked to harm and a need for fewer policemen, jails, and prisons if none were drunk.

l: messages, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Messages travel along separate nerve threads so they do not become mixed or confused. When a finger touches a hot stove, a message tells the brain that the finger will burn, and the brain sends a message to the muscles to contract, bend the joint, and pull the finger away.

l: tooth, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Teeth are bone covered with enamel and furnished with nerve. Different kinds do different work: front teeth cut food and back teeth grind it. They need cleanliness, careful brushing, and protection from cracking nuts or biting thread.

l: mouth, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The mouth contains saliva that helps prepare food before it reaches the stomach. Tobacco can make the mouth dry, discolor the teeth, and cause bad sores.

l: drunkards, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A drunkard is a person who keeps taking increasing amounts of alcohol-containing drinks, progressing from cider, wine, or beer to whiskey, brandy, or rum; alcohol injures the brain and nerves, impairing awareness.

l: grape-juice, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Grape-juice is squeezed from ripe grapes, drawn off from skins and seeds, and left in a warm place. Its sugar changes into alcohol and gas, developing bubbles; it contains water and becomes wine, no longer safe as a drink or suitable for making jelly.

l: sugar, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Sugar is a food and a fat-making food, found in ripe fruit-juices and coming from sugar-cane, maple-trees, beets, and starch. Starch changes into sugar as fruit ripens, when grain sprouts, and when saliva acts on food; then sugar can mix with blood and help feed the body. It feeds sprouting grain through roots and stems, but alone cannot prevent starvation. In standing grape-juice or apple-juice, or with yeast, it changes into alcohol and gas.

l: car bon'ic acid gas, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Carbonic acid gas moves in little bubbles in grape-juice, rises to the top of the liquid, then goes off into the air.

l: water, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Water is a substance needed for the body and used in preparing food. It may come from clouds, cisterns, springs, wells, and food, and is carried to houses through pipes. When boiled, it becomes steam; steam touching a cold plate or tin cover becomes drops of water again, allowing distilling. It does not burn, but water from lead pipes or wells near drains or stables may be poisonous or make people sick.

l: grapes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: When ripe, grapes contain water, sugar, and grape flavor; they are good food, can be squeezed for juice, which can change into wine.

l: wine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Wine is changed grape-juice containing water, alcohol, and grape flavor. It can also be made from currants, elderberries, and other fruits in much the same way as from grapes. It contains a little alcohol compared with distilled liquor, costs more than beer, and can be used to make distilled liquors, wine-jelly, and wine-sauce. Its alcohol may lead drinkers to become drunkards; if left warm long enough, it turns into vinegar.

l: cider, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Cider is a beverage made from crushed apples after apple-juice is pressed out. Soon, its sugar begins changing into alcohol and gas; it contains a little alcohol, though large amounts can provide much alcohol and may lead to drunkenness. It can often make drinkers ill-tempered and cross, may lead toward stronger liquors, and turns into vinegar if left warm long enough.

l: mind, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Mind, owned by every person and the best strength, is impaired by alcohol, which aches the head, deadens nerves, and hinders thinking.

l: alcoholic fermentation of fruit juice, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Alcoholic fermentation of fruit juice is the change of sugar in grape-juice or apple-juice into alcohol and bubbles of gas. Yeast helps the change; bubbles show it is progressing. Alcohol remains in the juice, while gas rises into the air.

l: grains, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Grain contains starch; when kept moist and warm and sprouting, its starch begins turning into sugar.

l: starch, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Starch is a food found in bread and all kinds of grain. It changes into sugar when seeds sprout, supporting beer from barley, and during chewing saliva changes it into sugar before it can enter the blood.

l: sprouting grain, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_a malt CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.] Sprouting grain is kept warm and moist so that its starch can turn into sugar. The brewer stops the sprouting before the sugar is used to feed the growing root and stem.

l: barley, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Barley is a grain containing starch, used by the brewer to make beer and liquor, and can be ground into barley-cakes or pearl barley for food.

l: brewer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A brewer makes malt by sprouting barley in a warm, moist place and stopping to save sugar, then soaks it in water, adds yeast and sometimes hops, and watches bubbles as sugar changes into gas and alcohol to make beer.

l: malt, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Malt is sprouting grain, soaked in water; brewer adds yeast to change its sugar into gas and alcohol.

l: food, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Food includes beef and supplies the body with water, lime, salt, flesh-making substances, and fat-making substances. Much comes from the earth through grains, grass, vegetables, and animals that eat them. Meat, vegetables, and bread require cooking; food is then chewed, swallowed, cut and ground by teeth, mixed with gastric juice, and changed and worked over in the stomach. The liver and other organs partly prepare it for passage from the intestines into the blood. Blood carries it to every part of the body, feeding bones, muscles, nerves, brain, skin, finger nails, hair, and eyes. It makes and mends bone, helps children grow, repairs worn-out parts in grown people, and, when good and simple, supports strength. Good food helps make good blood; named foods serve muscles, fat, and heat.

l: boy who drinks alcoholic beverages, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A boy at the same age and school as an abstaining boy drinks wine, cider, and beer. Alcohol poisons his body and mind, making him different from the abstaining boy and less likely to be chosen for good work or trusted with an engine or bank.

l: boy who abstains from alcoholic beverages, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A boy abstains from wine, cider, beer, and all alcoholic beverages, never letting them pass his lips; by avoiding alcohol’s harm to body and mind, he is presented as having a better chance in life.

l: alcohol poisoning, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Alcohol poisoning poisons the body and mind of the boy who drinks wine, cider, and beer; the boy who abstains does not suffer it.

l: distilling, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Distilling is a tea-kettle process in the kitchen that boils liquid into vapor, then condenses it back into liquid, producing distilled water or stronger alcohol.

l: steam, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Steam is water turned into vapor by boiling; when touching something cold, it changes back into water and is collected for observation.

l: vapor, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_used_in_place_of steam [when discussing boiling alcohol] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.] Vapor is the term used instead of steam when discussing the boiling of alcohol. Alcohol vapor is collected first because alcohol requires less heat to vaporize than water requires to turn into steam.

l: brandy, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Brandy is a distilled liquor from wine, nearly one-half alcohol, presented as a possible later stage after weaker alcoholic drinks.

l: rum, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Rum is a distilled liquor made from molasses and containing nearly or about one-half alcohol. It may follow weaker alcoholic drinks. Sailors once received it daily, with extra during great storms, but a captain found it did not make them stronger.

l: whiskey, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Whiskey is distilled liquor nearly one-half alcohol, costs more than beer, and is presented as a later stage after weaker alcoholic drinks.

l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Alcohol looks like water. When a lighted match is held near it, it burns with a blue flame that gives much heat but little light and makes no smoke or soot. It preserves dead bodies from decaying and is contained in various drinks, though pure alcohol is not often used as a drink. As its amount increases, danger increases. It is a poison: after entering the blood, it affects the brain and then the nerves, deadens nerves, impairs the mind, damages muscles, and can make the heart beat too fast, tire it, and become fatty. It cannot make good muscles, bone, nerve, or brain or give real strength; instead, it may encourage people to take more, make them imagine they can do more, and later leave them weaker. Habitual use can impair the five senses, cause trembling hands, confused nerves, thick speech, difficulty walking straight, or seeing things not present.

l: body heat, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Body heat comes from continuous work inside the body, is carried by blood to every part, and continually passes off through skin and breath.

l: tree-toad (in the bottle of alcohol), Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The tree-toad was put in a bottle of alcohol years ago and remains there, preserved from decay and looking as it did on the first day.

l: drinker, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: wants_more alcoholic drinks [often as consumption increases] A drinker may be deceived into thinking that taking more alcohol will be good for him. The more he takes, the more he often wants, and he may progress from cider, wine, or beer to whiskey, brandy, or rum.

l: appetite for alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_formed in childhood [sometimes] An appetite for alcohol may sometimes be formed in childhood. It can strongly beg for the poison, especially after a person learns to like the taste of alcohol.

l: farmer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: plants fields [with tobacco instead of corn, wheat, and potatoes] The farmer changed his crops from corn, wheat, and potatoes to tobacco. He dried the tobacco leaves and had them made into cakes, cigars, and snuff.

l: nicotine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Nicotine is a strong poison found in tobacco; one drop can kill a dog, and the amount in one cigar, if taken pure, could kill two men.

l: poison, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The text describes nicotine as a poison. A person may take in small amounts of it through smoking, but repeated exposure is not safe or truly helpful.

l: snuff mill, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: stands_beside stream [the stream turns the mill-wheel] The snuff mill stood beside a stream in a pleasant place with trees, fresh air, and open windows. Despite its surroundings, the tobacco smell was so strong that a visitor repeatedly went outside for pure air, and the worker said the smell had made him sick at first.

l: smoking and tobacco use, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Smoking and other tobacco use contain nicotine and make air unfit to breathe through smoke and strong bad smell; they offer no real help and can be unsafe, though cigar smoking does not usually kill immediately.

l: first-use sickness, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: First-use sickness is the body's warning after initial smoking or tobacco use: it signals danger and poison, then may disappear as the body becomes used to tobacco.

l: taking nicotine or poison repeatedly, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Taking small amounts of nicotine or poison day after day is unsafe and not helpful to anyone throughout.

l: soothing-syrup, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Soothing-syrup contains opium and is given to babies to stop crying, but it injures their tender nerves, poisons their bodies, and is a dangerous enemy rather than true comfort.

l: baby, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: has_part nerves [tender] A baby may be given soothing-syrup to quiet it, but the opium in the syrup can injure its tender nerves and poison its body. The text says that babies should receive patient and kind care instead.

l: organs, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_a part of the body [with special work to do] An organ is a part of the body that has some special work to do. The eye is the organ of sight, and the stomach takes care of the food people eat.

l: the eyes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The eyes are organs of sight: with a pupil and nerve of sight, they take pictures all day, sending accounts to the brain. Their delicate nerves need care and protection from bright or insufficient light and careless actions.

l: stomach, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The stomach is an organ that takes care of food: a strong bag with muscular walls and a lining that prepares gastric juice. After swallowing, it works food over, squeezing, rolling, and mixing it with gastric juice until it becomes a thin, grayish fluid. It prepares this food for the blood to take and sends it toward the intestines. It needs rest and warmth; alcohol, or hurriedly swallowed food, can harm it or cause aching.

l: enamel, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Enamel is a hard, smooth covering over tooth bone; it often breaks from cracking nuts, after which the tooth decays and aches and cannot receive new enamel.

l: chest, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Chest is the upper room of the bony box, formed by spine, ribs, shoulder-blades, and collar-bones, containing heart and lungs.

l: abdomen, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Abdomen is the lower room of the bony case, containing the stomach, liver, and other organs.

l: liver, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The liver partly prepares food.

l: gastric juice, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Gastric juice is prepared by the lining of the stomach and kept ready for use; it mixes with food, changing it into a thin, grayish fluid, but alcohol injures it.

l: milk, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Milk is the best kind of food, supplying lime for bones and helping make muscle and fat.

l: salt, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Salt is needed by people and animals, mixed with food or sought by cows, sheep, wild cattle, and buffaloes.

l: gastric digestion, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: changes food [into a thin, grayish fluid] Gastric digestion changes eaten food into a form that can be carried through the body and used to feed its parts. It depends on the teeth doing their work, the stomach being warm and rested, and the gastric juice mixing with the food.

l: skin, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Skin covers the body externally and lines it internally in a more delicate form. It has a thin protective outside layer over true skin full of nerves, pores, and perspiration tubes. These tubes carry away waste matter and water, supporting health, while skin loses body heat to cooler air. Washing with soap and water keeps pores unclogged and skin fresh and healthy.

l: saliva, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Saliva is a juice in the mouth. It moistens and mixes food during chewing, helps prepare it before it enters the stomach, and changes starch into sugar before the food can be taken into the blood. When tobacco juice is spit out, needed saliva is also lost.

l: flesh-making foods, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Flesh-making foods are needed by muscles and include milk, wheat, corn, oats, meat, and eggs.

l: fat-making foods, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Fat-making foods include sugar, starch, cream, rice, butter, and fat meat; they provide fat needed to keep the body warm and comfortable.

l: candy, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Candy is sugar, though some contains cheaper white earth. It may give children too much sugar, may be poisonous, and is not a complete food alone. Pure sugar candy dissolves completely in water; white earth remains at the bottom.

l: dinner, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Dinner includes roast beef, vegetables, bread, butter, salt, water, and fruits; after digestion, it can help make and mend different parts of the body.

l: cooking, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Cooking prepares meat, vegetables, and bread to be easily worked upon by the mouth and stomach; good cooking supports health, and well-cooked food is worth twice as much as poorly cooked food.

l: chewing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Chewing mixes saliva with food, changes starch into sugar, should be slow and thorough, and precedes swallowing.

l: swallowing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Swallowing is a process that moves food down the throat into the stomach through the passage behind the windpipe, safely when the windpipe’s trap-door shuts; speaking while eating may cause choking.

l: blood, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Blood is a body fluid made from good food. It takes prepared food from the intestines or stomach to the heart, which pumps it through the lungs and throughout the body. As it flows through arteries and thousands of little branches, it carries food and body heat to every part, leaving material needed for making and mending body parts. Work inside the body warms it; faster flow brings more heat. Blood also gathers and carries away worn-out matter. After collecting impurities, it becomes dull and bluish and returns by veins to the heart. The lungs use fresh air to purify it, making it bright and pure again, after which it is sent to the heart and pumped out once more. It must be good and pure for the brain, though alcohol or tobacco can poison it.

l: digestion and nutrition, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: includes food [as it becomes part of the body] The unit describes digestion and nutrition as the preparation of food by cooking, chewing, saliva, the stomach, and the intestines, followed by its transport in the blood. This process supplies the body with material to make and repair its parts.

l: strength, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_a physical capacity Strength is gained by eating good, simple food, exercising in the open air, and taking pure air into the lungs. Alcohol does not give real strength, and the feeling of strength it produces lasts only a little while.

l: captain, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A captain observes rum weakening sailors, then leads a voyage without it, providing plentiful food and hot coffee during storms.

l: sailors, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Sailors once received daily and storm-time rum, but after an ocean crossing without it, with good food and hot coffee, reported stronger feelings and better work.

l: ship, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: carries rum [by the former customary practice] Ships were once expected to carry a great deal of rum for sailors. One captain took a ship to sea without rum and found that the sailors worked better and felt stronger.

l: alcohol and strength, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Alcohol opposes strength: it cannot build muscles, bone, nerve, or brain, briefly dulls nerves to create a false feeling, then decreases strength.

l: strength of body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Strength of body is measured by raising a weight over a pulley and is gained through open-air exercise, pure air, and good, simple food.

l: artery, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_a tube [carries blood away from the heart] Arteries are tubes through which the heart pumps blood. They have thousands of little branches that extend throughout the body.

l: veins, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Veins are tubes that bring blood back to the heart; some smaller veins are visible in the wrist.

l: pulse, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Pulse is the steady beating felt by pressing a finger on an artery in the wrist; it indicates how fast the heart pumps and blood flows, and a doctor feels it when someone is sick.

l: fresh air, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Fresh air enables lungs to work and purify blood; it is needed fresh and plentiful, but waste matter breathed out poisons it, and when it cannot enter a room, people may feel dull, sleepy, or have headache.

l: worn-out matter, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Waste matter is carried away from the body through skin and other ways, passes through perspiration tubes, and should be washed off to prevent clogged pores.

l: clothing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Clothing is worn next to the skin and keeps body heat from escaping while blocking cold air. Tight clothing can restrict lungs; after wear it contains worn-out particles and should be aired. For cold weather, it includes woolen under-garments, thick boots, and stockings.

l: breathing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Breathing occurs day and night without stopping, with short pauses between breaths that rest the lungs; nose breathing is better because nose hairs catch dust and impurities.

l: perspiration, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Perspiration is water drops appearing on the skin through pores from inside the body. Produced continually in winter and summer, it carries water and waste matter out through the skin.

l: work of the body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: includes stomach digestion [one of four important kinds of work] The work of the body includes the stomach preparing food, the blood carrying food and removing worn-out matter, the lungs using fresh air to purify the blood, and the skin carrying away waste matter. This work continues day and night without conscious thought because nerves send messages to the muscles.

l: the five senses, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The five senses are ways of learning about things around a person, including sight, touch, taste, smell, and hearing.

l: sight, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Sight is one of the five senses and depends on the eyes and the nerve of sight. Its delicate nerves can be harmed by too much or too little light.

l: hearing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Hearing is one of the five senses and depends on the ears and the nerve of hearing. It can be harmed by putting hard or sharp objects into the ears.

l: the pupil, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The pupil is a round, black opening in the middle of the eye, with a muscle around it; it lets in light, becoming smaller in bright light and larger in darkness.

l: the nerve of sight, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The delicate nerve of sight, behind the pupil, carries accounts of everything seen to the brain, can be harmed by bright light or trying to see in dark, and does not regrow after being killed.

l: the light, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: can_harm the nerve of sight [when it is too bright] The light should be sufficient for reading and studying but should not be faced directly when it is very bright. While writing, it should come from the left side so that the hand's shadow does not fall on the work.

l: the ears, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The visible ears are curved pieces of gristle that catch sounds and pass them to the true ears deeper in the head; they require care, including washing with a soft towel and avoiding hard or sharp objects.

l: the nerve of hearing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: sends_to the brain [an account of each sound] The nerve of hearing is deeper in the head and sends an account of each sound to the brain. It is in less danger than the nerve of sight, but it can be injured when a pin breaks the ear's drum.

l: the boys who looked at the sun, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: A group of boys foolishly compete to look longest at the sun; all suffer brain and eye harm, and the boy who looks longest dies.

l: the boy who made himself cross-eyed, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: has eyes that are not quite set right [despite painful work by doctors] The boy tried to imitate a schoolmate who was cross-eyed by turning his own eyes. He could not turn them back properly, and doctors were never able to set them quite right despite painful treatment.

l: the boy's father, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: suffers_from the earache [recurrently after childhood] The boy's father laid his ear against a door crack to feel the wind blow into it when he was young. He afterward suffered severe earache and often had earache throughout his life.

l: care of the eyes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Care of the eyes emphasizes avoiding direct bright light and strain, using sufficient light for reading, and placing light on the left while writing; it warns against sun-gazing, twilight reading, and crossing the eyes.

l: heat and cold, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: is_a a subject concerning body warmth and cooling Heat is produced by work inside the body and is carried throughout it by the blood. Cold causes heat to be lost, especially when cool air carries it away from the skin.

l: Arctic explorers, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: report alcohol does not keep them warm [in very cold countries] Arctic explorers report that alcohol does not keep them warm. They travel through icy regions, sometimes use dog sledges and Esquimau huts, and may drink oil and eat walrus meat.

l: Greely party, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The Greely party was a group of twenty-six men in an Arctic ordeal. After months of starvation and freezing in the Arctic seas, nineteen died; seven were rescued alive, though one soon died.

l: Arctic expedition ordeal, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: caused nineteen deaths [among the Greely party] The Greely party's ordeal involved months of hunger and extreme cold in the Arctic seas. Most of the men died, while those who survived generally had not used tobacco or had used it only seldom.

l: cold exposure and freezing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: can_be_caused_by alcohol use [because alcohol increases heat loss and deadens warning sensations] Cold exposure causes the body to lose heat and can lead to freezing and death. Alcohol may make freezing happen more quickly because it increases heat loss and prevents a person from recognizing the danger.

l: money, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: becomes wasted money [when spent for that which will do no good, but only harm] Money can be saved or spent in good and pleasant ways, but spending it on liquor or tobacco wastes it. A dollar spent on two mugs of beer a day is wasted in ten days.

l: cost of alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: The cost of alcohol can quickly use up a dollar: two mugs of beer a day consume a dollar in ten days, while wine or whiskey use it sooner because they cost more.

l: cost of tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: amounts_to six hundred million dollars [yearly in this country] The yearly cost of tobacco in the country is six hundred million dollars. This money is described as burned up, wasted, and worse than wasted.

l: six hundred million dollars, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Six hundred million dollars are spent yearly in this country for tobacco, described as money burned up, wasted, and worse than wasted.

l: pronunciation codes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Pronunciation codes are marked in the text by breve, macron, tilde, or slash through a letter.

l: Jane Andrews, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes
s: Jane Andrews is identified as the author of Child's Health Primer For Primary Classes.
